Front Office Leaderboard · Active MLB Regimes

Value added vs. expectation across the six acquisition channels, realized WAR only, per season of tenure. Letter grades (hover any grade for its 20–80 scouting-scale value). FOR rates decision quality; Success rates on-field results; the gap between them is a story in itself. Dev rates player development: prospect value created while in the org, marked-to-market from the MLB Pipeline top-100 archive (2011-2026), with credit staying home even when the prospect is later traded. Every value on this board is computed by Ledger WAR v1.5, our self-built metric from the live MLB Stats API feed: park factors (home/away run environments, 3-yr rolling), SABR Defensive Index and Statcast defense, framing, and baserunning, under sweep v2 (control windows, win-curve leverage, time discounting). The Dodgers, Orioles, and Brewers cards additionally carry hand-verified curated decision pages. Extensions are graded against the extension market for the player's service class, not FA prices (locking up Acuña cheap is the skill; the pre-arb discount itself is structural). Qualifying-offer signings carry a draft-compensation charge, and deferral-heavy deals are costed at CBT value. Free agency is graded against 1,630 real contracts (ESPN tables 2006-2021 + curated recent winters through 2025-26); regimes with fewer than 8 matched deals stay pending ('·'). The Era filter adds 71 archive regimes (2005-2024), scored by the same engine over their actual windows.

Methodology (abridged)

The unit of account is the decision: a dated transaction attributed to the executive regime in office when it was made. Each decision is scored in WAR captured (production received during the club-control window acquired) and surplus dollars (WAR × market $/WAR, minus salary paid). Departing players are scored symmetrically, so every deal nets to one number.

Grading against expectation, not zero

Draft picks are measured against the historical expected value of their slot; the #1 overall pick carries a far higher bar than pick #38. Prospects moved in trades are valued at the deal date using published prospect-tier surplus curves, so the ledger can score a trade both as it looked at the time and as it turned out; the gap between the two is the luck-versus-skill diagnostic. Free agency is graded as return on the market price of the contract, and the waiver/minor-league channel is graded against a baseline of zero: pure found money, the cleanest read on pro scouting. Net-of-cost is the universal display rule wherever a contract exists: FA signings and extensions never show raw WAR accumulation, because signing a star who then plays like a star is a pass, not a triumph.

Lenses, and open vs. closed

Every substantial decision is shown through a stack of named lenses rather than one verdict: windows-only (the control years actually exchanged), option-inclusive (adding retention rights and their exercise), and the counterfactual (this regime against its own realistic alternative), with raw v0.1 and leverage-adjusted v0.2 readings where they differ. Perspective rule: every lens on a regime's card is signed from that regime's seat. The other side of the same deal grades on the other regime's card, from theirs; the Betts trade reads as Friedman's win on Friedman's card and as Bloom's defensible sale on Boston's, and both are correct because each is measured against its own alternative. Alongside the lenses, every decision and every branch of a transaction tree carries a status: CLOSED means the window is finished and the number is final; OPEN means value is still accruing and the verdict can move. The site never averages the lenses into one number; the disagreement between them is the analysis.

Transaction trees

Assets compound across decisions: a fourth-round pick becomes a rental ace becomes a comp pick becomes a new draftee. The Trees view follows these chains generation by generation, marking each branch open or closed, with captured value in solid cards and outflows in dashed ones. Trees are also the honest way to display sell-offs: the Orioles' 2025 deadline reads as a dozen open branches, not a graded verdict.

Win-curve leverage & time discounting (v0.2)

A marginal win is worth 3–4× more at 89 projected wins than at 70 or 105, so acquired WAR is multiplied by a leverage curve, L(w) = 0.5 + 1.3·e−(w−89)²/200, peaking at 1.80, evaluated at the acquirer's projected wins on the decision date: the front office is graded on the leverage it thought it was buying. Future-year value discounts to the decision date at 10%/yr (6–14% sensitivity shown): a 2029 prospect win was never worth a 2024 pennant-race win to a defending champion, and win-now is a rational preference the ledger must price, not a bias to correct. Together these fixed v0.1's systematic bias (deadline buys punished, sell-side hauls flattered) and flipped the Burnes trade from "worst decision of the tenure" (−2.9) to a fair playoff-push price (+1.2). Every parameter (curve shape, discount rate, projected wins per case) is versioned and public.

Retention rights & opportunity cost

A trade transfers a third asset beyond the control windows: the exclusive right to extend the player. Pricing it at zero produces indefensible verdicts: the windows-only ledger says Boston "won" the Betts trade. Every trade therefore shows three ledgers: windows-only; option-inclusive (realized extension surplus flows to the acquirer once the right is exercised, the headline number); and the seller's counterfactual, charged p(retain) × forfeited extension surplus, where p is a documented, versioned judgment drawn from negotiation reporting. The same machinery scores passive retention failures (letting a star walk is charged p-weighted forfeited surplus with the comp pick credited), so "traded him with team control left" and "let him leave for nothing" become directly comparable. Under this accounting deals stop being zero-sum: in the Betts case both front offices beat their realistic alternatives, which is the honest and more interesting answer.

The rental market (v0.3)

The lens stack now has an empirical anchor: 237 deadline rental deals classified exactly from the league feed (acquired June-August, declared free agency within five months), with the buyer's receipt measured as rest-of-season Ledger WAR and the price as what the surrendered players actually became for the seller. Findings: a star rental win costs about 0.8 realized wins; the median deadline rental costs approximately nothing that ever materializes; and more than half of rental buys deliver under 0.3 wins. With a market price in hand, a trade grades on two questions: paid vs. the market at the time, and realized vs. paid. Applied to the canonical case: Boston's return for one expected year of Betts was roughly market rate; the ledger's criticism was never the price, it is the decision to be a seller of that asset at all. Full study: methodology v0.3 addendum in the repo; the recent-era ratio is disclosed as right-censored while surrendered prospects mature.

The controlled-years market (v0.4)

The complement of the rental study: 1,372 deadline deals 2005-2023 where acquired players came with control beyond the season, with control measured from the feed (seasons until the player's first free-agency declaration, capped at six). The price curve by control: one extra year of control trades at about 1.0 wins paid per win received (the deadline premium on controlled players is real and larger than the 0.8 star-rental rate); two extra years at ~0.86; and the three-plus bucket, which is mostly the seller's seat buying prospect packages, at ~0.37 paid per win eventually received, with a 71% bust rate. In other words: sellers buy future wins at about a third of the price buyers pay for present ones, and they pay for that discount in variance. The biggest controlled buys in the archive (Turner, Arrieta, Verlander, Gallen, the Soto package) were all acquired at single-digit prices against double-digit returns. Full tables in data/rental_market.json.

Player development (DEV)

Development is a third top-level grade beside FOR and Success, because turning a 16-year-old into a top-100 prospect is neither an acquisition nor an on-field result. Prospects are marked to market on a rank-to-surplus-wins curve using the MLB Pipeline top-100 archive (2011-2026, 1,548 rank-rows), with the holding org derived from minor-league rosters, not the rankings. Entry credit is net of acquisition cost (own draft pick vs. the pick-value curve; own international signing; acquired as prospect) with an inherited screen: a prospect developed to the list under a predecessor earns the new regime nothing at entry. Rank moves accrue to the org holding the player, graduation to MLB is a neutral exit, and falling off without debuting is charged. Credit stays home when the prospect is later traded, which is the point. Grades are league-relative because development is positive-sum (about +2.5 wins of prospect value per club-season league-wide).

Extensions, the sixth channel

An extension is not a free-agent signing: the club shops the extension market for that service class, which trades at a deep structural discount to open-market $/win. Grading Acuña's 8/$100M against FA prices would call every pre-arb extension a triumph; grading it against what pre-arb extensions typically pay isolates the skill. Class discounts (pre-debut 0.35, early 0.45, arb 0.60, veteran 0.90 of market $/win) are documented assumptions, tunable as the book grows. Deferral-heavy deals are costed at CBT/present value (Betts $306.7M, and Ohtani $460.8M in the FA channel), and qualifying-offer signings carry a draft-compensation charge, because the pick surrendered is a baseball asset even when the dollars are ownership's.

Attribution rules

A regime is graded only on its own decisions; inherited players are excluded. Extensions, non-tenders, and passive losses (a free agent walking, a player lost on waivers) are decisions too. Recent regimes carry a small-sample badge rather than being hidden, and the leaderboard defaults to realized value only, with projected-remaining value shown separately. Every rating is clickable down to the individual decisions that produced it, and every methodology version is archived so grades are reproducible. The two Betts decisions on the Dodgers card are scored with real data as a proof of concept; the trade and the extension are separate, chainable decisions, and that one example shows why: on windows alone the deal reads as an overpay, while the full chain reads as one of the great decisions of the era. Same inputs, different lenses, both on the page.

Two grades, on purpose

FOR (Front Office Rating) measures decision quality: value added versus expectation across the six channels. Team Success measures on-field results during the tenure: winning percentage, division titles, playoff appearances, playoff series wins, pennants, and World Series. They are deliberately separate: a front office can out-decide the league and still miss Octobers (payroll, luck, timing), or ride inherited stars to banners. The gap between the two grades is often the most interesting number on the page. Grades display as letters (A+ through F) mapped from the underlying 20–80 scouting scale, which stays available on hover.

Validation: does the metric hold up?

Two checks, both reproducible from the public feed. Accounting: a WAR-class metric must sum to team record. Across 327 team-seasons (2015-2025), roster-summed Ledger WAR v1.5 vs actual wins above a 48-win replacement baseline: correlation 0.861, R² 0.741, slope 0.850, mean absolute error 5.2 wins. (Two things got it there: park factors in v1.5, and the archive sweep's full 2005+ player universe, which filled out role players the current-regime cache had never needed to value. Fuller rosters sum closer to truth, which is itself evidence the metric is additive the way WAR must be.) The slope below 1 reflects known gaps (defense coverage thins before 2016; pre-2014 seasons are bat-plus-position only), which are disclosed rather than patched. Prediction: does decision quality carry information about FUTURE results beyond the current record? Pooled across 134 regime-years, net decision value per season through year t predicts the next two seasons' winning percentage with a partial correlation of 0.338 after controlling for the record to date, lifting R² from 0.282 to 0.364. Decision quality is not just a scorecard of the past; it is forward information the standings do not contain. (Pooled regime-years overlap, so significance is overstated by the raw n; the effect size is the claim, not the p-value.)

What this machinery does inside a front office

This site is the public, free-data build of a decision-support system. Pointed at a club's internal data, the same machinery gives you: deadline pricing (the live rental-market curve says what a win costs this July, and whether an offer is above or below the market that actually clears); extension pricing (the class-market baselines say what the comparable pre-arb or arb extension really costs, with CBT-aware deferral valuation); counterparty preparation (every GM's trade record, channel tendencies, buy-low habits, and development effects, so you know who overvalues what before the call); self-audit (which of your channels is actually producing, process-vs-outcome separation so you stop firing scouts for variance); and regime benchmarking for ownership. Swap Ledger WAR for your internal projections and the prospect-rank archive for your own pref lists and every grade sharpens; nothing in the architecture assumes public data, it was simply built to prove the concept without any.

About this project

Built by Sean Zerillo as a working demonstration: a complete decision-level accounting system for front-office performance, from raw transaction feed to graded, clickable, versioned product, with every number computed from free public data. The stack is deliberately simple (Python ingestion and scoring, SQLite, a single-file front end, zero frameworks, zero scraping of licensed sources) so the methodology, not the engineering, is the point. Everything is reproducible from the public repository, including this page. Contact: sean.zerillo@gmail.com.

Retention v2 (in the composite)

Raw leakage (wins produced elsewhere by departed free agents) scales with how many stars a club employs, so it was display-only in v1: it graded payroll, not decisions. v2 conditions on who left. From every free-agency departure league-wide 2005-2023, we build the empirical curve of what departures of each caliber go on to do over the next three seasons (a 2-win departure returns ~1.0; a 10-win departure ~5.2). A regime is graded only on the gap between its departures' actual next-three-years and that expectation, plus a +1.0 win compensation-pick credit per qualifying-offer walkaway (mirroring the QO charge on the signing club's FA ledger). The channel is centered at zero by construction (league mean +0.1) and now joins the FOR composite. Letting a six-win player walk is not a mistake; repeatedly letting the ones walk who still had the most left is. Departures after 2023 are right-censored (their next three seasons are not observable yet) and excluded, disclosed.

Historical depth

The ledger is designed to backfill decade by decade; transactions exist back to the 1870s (Retrosheet), so historical regimes (Weiss, Rickey, Schuerholz, Gillick) sit on the same scale as active ones. Channel definitions adapt by era: before the 1965 amateur draft, the "draft" channel reads as amateur and international signings. Era-specific $/WAR baselines keep cross-era comparisons honest.

Data status: the leaderboard, all 27 active cards badged COMPUTED, and all 71 archive-regime cards are generated end-to-end by Ledger WAR v1.5 and the sweep engine from the live MLB Stats API feed (plus the curated Dodgers, Orioles, and Brewers cards, whose decision pages are hand-verified). Archive regimes (2005-2024) grade trade/draft/waiver channels over their actual windows; FA is shown raw and DEV/EXT are not scored for past windows, disclosed on each card. Sample values persist only where labeled: parts of the curated decision pages, the curated Trees showcase, and the Champions tab's contribution estimates.
